column6: The commentary sends Musa on a road to Midian and then to its water; Exodus 2:15 sends fleeing Moses to Midian, where he sits by a well, supplying the same journey-to-well opening.
The commentary identifies two women unable to water their herds; Exodus 2:16 has seven daughters come to draw water and fill the troughs, giving the shared well scene its Israelite form.
The commentary says Musa waters the women’s flocks; Exodus 2:17 has Moses rise, defend the daughters from shepherds, and water their flock.

column5: who makes room at the well
column6: The commentary says the women wait for shepherds to leave and Musa then waters them; Exodus has Moses drive the shepherds off himself, shifting the aid from waiting and serving to direct intervention.
The commentary’s scene ends with Musa watering two women’s flocks; Exodus 2:19 has the daughters report that an Egyptian rescued them and drew water for them and their flock.

column5: traveler and camels at a well
column6: The commentary makes a road traveler’s water and a well central; Abraham’s servant reaches a town well with camels and waits there as women come to draw water.

column5: prayer for success at the well
column6: After Musa waters the women, the commentary quotes his prayer for whatever good God sends; Abraham’s servant prays at the well for success, making a water encounter the setting for a request for divine direction.

column5: women draw water at the spring
column6: The commentary centers women who come to a water source with flocks; the servant in Genesis stands by the spring as the city’s daughters come out to draw water.

column5: water for a stranger and his animals
column6: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks; Rebekah gives Abraham’s servant a drink and then draws for his camels, closely joining stranger, well, and animal water.

column5: water runs out in the wilderness
column6: The commentary asks who can bring running water when a person’s supply sinks away; Hagar’s water skin is empty in the wilderness, making thirst on a journey concrete.
The commentary asks who supplies water when it disappears; God opens Hagar’s eyes to a well, and she draws water for the child, a direct scene of provision after water runs out.

The commentary says Yusuf’s brothers propose the pit so a passing traveler may take him; Reuben instead proposes the pit to keep the brothers from killing Joseph, a shared rescue-through-the-pit plan with a changed rationale.

The commentary describes Yusuf thrown into the dark bottom of a well before travelers arrive; Genesis has Joseph put into an empty cistern, matching the pit while withholding the Qur’anic water-drawing detail.
The commentary’s next Yusuf scene has a bucket lowered to draw water and a boy discovered; Genesis explicitly says Joseph’s cistern was empty, making the means of discovery differ.

column5: caravan and the boy in the pit
column6: The commentary says a caravan arrives and its water drawer finds Yusuf; Genesis has traders pass and Joseph brought up from the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites, sharing the pit-and-caravan turn.

column5: water from the ground sustains land
column6: The commentary distinguishes rain from above and well water drawn from below; Genesis 2:6 pictures mist rising from the ground to water the soil before cultivated growth.
The commentary links water to vegetation and livelihood; Genesis 2:10 describes a river flowing from Eden to water the garden, locating plant life beside a sustaining source.
The commentary follows rain into soil and plants; Deuteronomy contrasts a land that drinks rain from heaven with Egypt’s irrigation, making rainfall the land’s source of fertility.
The commentary traces rain to vegetation and provision; Deuteronomy promises rain at its proper season so grain, wine, and oil can grow.
The commentary’s cloud and rain enlarge the earth with plant growth; Leviticus promises seasonal rain followed by a land that yields produce and trees that bear fruit.

column5: springs and streams in good land
column6: The commentary pairs the traveler’s road with water and treats water as the support of livelihood; Deuteronomy describes a land of brooks, springs, and deep waters that sustains its inhabitants.

column5: tree beside streams, leaf does not wither

column5: the righteous way and the perishing way

The commentary links rain with mercy and the revival of soil; Psalm 65 says God visits and waters the earth, filling the divine river and preparing grain.

column5: showers soften furrows and bless growth

The commentary connects hamd with rain and the earth’s fertility; Psalm 104 begins in praise and then describes God’s care of clouds, mountains, plants, and food.

The commentary follows rain into tender plants and fields; Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for people to cultivate.

column5: food and drink from the earth
column6: The commentary links water to livelihood and food; Psalm 104 names wine, oil, and bread as gifts that gladden, nourish, and strengthen human life.

column5: cloud, rain, and grass in one verse
column6: The commentary links clouds and moisture to plant growth; Psalm 147 says God covers the heavens with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the hills.

The commentary places hamd beside rain and mercy; Psalm 147’s call to sing with thanksgiving leads directly into its account of clouds, rain, grass, and animal food.

column5: rain’s work and the effective word
column6: The commentary describes rain as a mark written into the earth and asks for guidance; Isaiah compares the word from God’s mouth to rain that does not return before accomplishing its purpose.

The commentary says the first rain marks earth with plants; Isaiah pictures descendants springing up like grass and willows beside flowing water.
The commentary says rain writes its mark in green growth and asks for guidance; Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew that fall on tender grass, making the same image a vehicle for instruction.
The commentary describes clouds that carry water and grow plants; Job says God draws up drops of water and distills rain from the mist.
The commentary develops the cloud as a layered bearer of rain; Job says clouds pour down water upon humankind.

column5: wind, clouds, and rain in sequence
column6: The commentary says winds move and spread clouds before rain; Jeremiah says God makes clouds rise, flashes lightning for rain, and brings wind from storehouses.

column5: wind and rain from God’s storehouses
column6: The commentary pairs wind, heavy cloud, and rainfall; Psalm 135 gives the same cluster as God’s work, bringing clouds, lightning for rain, and winds from storehouses.

The commentary’s ribba is a plant that does not wither in summer; Ezekiel’s trees beside the river bear fruit every month and keep leaves that do not wither.
The commentary asks who can bring running water when it sinks away; Jeremiah calls God the fountain of living waters and condemns people who abandon it for cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.
The commentary says water is the support by which affairs stand; Psalm 46’s river gladdens God’s city, where God’s presence keeps it from being moved.

The commentary asks to be guided on the straight road; Jesus says the way to life is narrow and difficult and few find it.

The commentary asks for the path of those granted favor rather than those under wrath; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.
The commentary distinguishes the favored from those under anger; the same judgment scene sends the cursed away, giving a concrete Christian counterpart to its divided outcome.

column5: guide to springs of living water
column6: The commentary joins guidance on a road to water for the traveler; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water.
The commentary calls water the support and “king” of human affairs; Revelation’s river of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, joining rule to life-giving water.
The commentary links gathered water to persistent vegetation; Revelation places the tree of life beside the river, bearing fruit and leaves for healing.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Revelation depicts the dead standing before the throne and being judged from the opened books according to their deeds.

The commentary brings cloud, travel, and water together; Paul recalls Israel’s ancestors under the cloud and on their wilderness passage, supplying the Christian pilgrimage setting for his water reference.

The commentary treats water as the literal support of the traveler; Paul rereads Israel’s wilderness drink from the rock as spiritual drink from Christ, adding a Christian interpretation to water on the journey.

column5: weary traveler rests at a well
column6: The commentary’s Musa reaches a well after travel and later withdraws to shade; Jesus, tired from his journey, sits beside Jacob’s well, a close Christian well-side travel scene.

column5: request for water at the well
column6: The commentary has Musa water women at Midian; Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink at Jacob’s well, making the well encounter turn on who gives water.

column5: ordinary well water becomes living water
column6: The commentary insists that a traveler’s water sustains his affairs; Jesus interprets the well encounter through the gift of living water, adding a spiritual reading to literal thirst.
The commentary follows rain and well water into enduring life; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring within the recipient, a Christian expansion from provision to lasting life.

column5: thirsty people are invited to come
column6: The commentary says water keeps the traveler from thirst and supports life; Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, turning thirst into a direct spiritual appeal.
The commentary traces water from source to soil and growth; Jesus describes rivers of living water flowing from the believer, extending the image from provision to inward abundance.

column5: seasonal mention of rain in prayer
column6: The commentary develops rain and wind as divine provision; the Mishnah debates when the rain petition enters the daily prayer cycle, showing rain as a recurring Jewish liturgical request.

column5: prayer formula for wind and rain
column6: The commentary joins wind, clouds, and rain; the Talmud explains the seasonal prayer formula that asks God to make wind blow and rain fall.

column5: rain and resurrection as divine acts
column6: The commentary cites a Qur’anic scene where rain-bearing clouds lead into the raising of the dead; the Talmud groups rain and resurrection among powers God has not delegated, giving the same pair a Jewish theological frame.

column5: sheep gone astray from their way
column6: The commentary asks not to follow those who stray and elsewhere describes flocks at the well; Isaiah says all sheep have gone astray, each turning to its own way, joining animal wandering to the path language.
The commentary makes rain a sign of divine benefit and renewal; Hosea compares God’s coming to dawn and to rain that waters the earth, giving the rain a covenantal and restorative meaning.
The commentary follows rain into green growth and provision; Joel promises early and late rains as part of restoration, tying weather to renewed harvest.
The commentary traces water toward food; Joel’s restoration scene has threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after the rains.

column5: ask for rain in its season
column6: The commentary’s imagery treats rain as provision from God; Zechariah explicitly tells people to ask the LORD for rain at the time of spring rain.
The commentary says rain improves people’s state and benefits them; Ezekiel promises showers of blessing, making rain a direct sign of restored divine care.

column5: prayer to be led in God’s truth
column6: The commentary’s central petition is “guide us” on a straight path; David asks God to lead him in truth and teach him, a close prayer-form parallel.
The commentary grounds guidance in divine favor and benefit; the psalm asks God to remember compassion and steadfast love, linking direction to mercy.
The commentary asks for the straight way; the psalm asks God’s good Spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, a specific guidance formula.

column5: rain falls on just and unjust
column6: The commentary says rain corrects people’s condition and benefits them while the surah distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Jesus says God gives rain to both just and unjust, making rain’s reach broader than the moral division.
The commentary opens with bism and develops its name/mark association; the Lord’s Prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, a parallel invocation before petitions.
The commentary calls God master of the Judgment Day; the Lord’s Prayer petitions for God’s kingdom and will, placing divine rule before requests for provision and guidance.
The commentary moves from rain and water to food for people and animals; the Lord’s Prayer asks for daily bread, making sustenance part of the prayer’s petition.

column5: lead away from trial and evil
column6: The commentary asks for the right path and exclusion from straying; the Lord’s Prayer asks not to be led into trial and to be delivered from evil, a neighboring petition for safe direction.
The commentary moves from invoking God’s name to divine rule and guidance; Luke’s Lord’s Prayer likewise begins with the Father’s name and kingdom before its requests.
The commentary follows rainwater into food and livelihood; Luke’s prayer asks for daily bread, placing provision within the same petitionary form.
The commentary asks to be guided away from a mistaken path; Luke’s prayer asks not to be brought into trial, a specific prayer for protection from a wrong course.
The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored by God from the paths of wrath and straying; the Didache opens its instruction with two ways, one of life and one of death.

column5: water from the rock on the way
column6: The commentary says water keeps a traveler’s work standing; Paul recalls Israel drinking from a spiritual rock in the wilderness, making provision on a journey the basis for a Christian reading.
The commentary calls water the support of affairs and traces it into food; Sirach lists water among the necessities of human life beside bread, fire, salt, and other provisions.

column5: Hebrew shem, name placed on people
column6: The commentary labels bism with a name-related source and then links it to wasm, a mark made by first rain; Numbers says the priests put God’s name upon Israel and God blesses them, joining name, marking, and benefit.

The commentary labels Qur’anic mālik from M-L-K and calls water “our kings”; Psalm 47 uses the cognate Hebrew melek for God as king over all earth, showing the sovereignty sense beyond the water metaphor.

The commentary labels mustaqim from Q-W-M and says water is what makes affairs stand; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew yaqumu for sinners who will not stand in judgment, connecting uprightness with the judgment scene.
The commentary’s N-ʿ-M family describes life’s beauty and freshness; Psalm 133 calls shared life good and pleasant with Hebrew na'im, a cognate use centered on what is delightful.

The commentary labels al-ʿālamīn from ʿ-L-M and also develops a deep, water-filled well from that family; the Peshitta uses cognate ʿālmā for “world,” showing the word’s spatial world sense in a Christian text.

The commentary calls the plant-growing cloud by the Qur’anic title Rabb; John preserves the Aramaic address rabbi and glosses it as teacher, showing a related Semitic master-title in a human teaching relation.

The commentary labels its cloud and tender-plant forms from R-B-B; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew revivim for showers falling on tender grass, a plausible cognate cluster whose exact lexical relationship should be checked in the Hebrew text.

The commentary labels hamd from Ḥ-M-D and says the earth is pleasing to inhabit or pasture; Psalm 19 calls the teaching desirable, a possible cognate that preserves a pleasing/desirable sense without equating it with praise.
